paper.title: Interactive Jewellery: a design exploration
paper.selectionReason: HCI layout and two-column conference variation

rows.source: Many current wearables have a technology-driven background: the focus is primarily on functionality, while their possible personal and social-cultural value is underappreciated. We think that developing wearables from a jewellery perspective can compensate for this. The personal and social cultural values embodied by traditional jewellery are often tightly connected to their function as memento. In this paper we reflect from a jewellery perspective, a memory-studies perspective and a TEI-perspective on three design proposals for interactive jewellery. We identify

rows.source: The framework that we sketched above describes jewellery in general. Even those who don’t wear jewellery themselves will recognise the personal and social cultural values of jewellery we described, as they are inherently part of human culture. In this first paragraph on related work we’ll focus on the less generally known segment of contemporary jewellery (see Den Besten [1:9–11] for an extensive reflections on possible labels for this segment). In the second half of the 20th century a growing group of jewellers in Western Europe [2] and North America [16] started to claim their creative independency and to challenge the general perception of jewellery [22]. At first the approaches differed hugely on both sides of the ocean [1:9], in recent decades contemporary jewellery has become a global scene. It would be impossible to give a complete overview of contemporary jewellery (for that, see [1,3,23]). Instead we present three examples that in different ways challenge the framework we sketched above.
